architecture.mechanism: Real-time active mass redistribution using a miniature movable counterweight driven by a micro‑actuator, guided by the imbalance sensor to counteract rotor asymmetry
architecture.intervention: Add a micro‑actuated counterweight system and a closed‑loop control algorithm that adjusts its position based on the imbalance sensor output, integrated into the spindle drive electronics
architecture.expected_effect: Measurable reduction in vibration amplitude and rotor speed ripple, enabling stable operation at higher speeds and improved separation consistency
architecture.falsification_test: Run the centrifuge with a deliberately introduced 5 g imbalance at maximum rated speed and verify that vibration exceeds the specified limit (e.g., >0.5 g RMS); if it does, the active balancing hypothesis is falsified

challenge.note: the fallback architecture has not faced the challenge gauntlet yet — the evolution loop challenges it in generation 2's evaluation path

preserved_objections.basis: the required micro‑actuator and closed‑loop control lack any demonstrated size, power, or response specifications, and the cited literature contains no evidence of such active mass redistribution in a compact benchtop centrifuge, violating physical feasibility.

adding a movable counterweight and actuator exceeds the compact, sealed, and safety‑circuit constraints defined for the benchtop module, breaking the boundary condition of a self‑contained low‑power device.

the referenced papers (DOI 10.1080/01496395.2019.1636820; 10.1007/978-1-4939-7271-5_19; 10.1016/j.bpj.2014.11.943; 10.1016/j.ohx.2022.e00328; 10.1097/01.bmsas.0000462030.15183.5d) describe passive benchtop centrifuges and provide no data on active balancing performance, directly contradicting the claim of measurable vibration reduction.

the standard benchtop centrifuge already satisfies the vibration limit (≤0.5 g RMS); the candidate’s prediction that a 5 g imbalance will exceed this limit is unsupported, making the hypothesis equivalent to the existing baseline.

integrating a miniature counterweight actuator, sensor, and control algorithm into the spindle drive electronics of a benchtop centrifuge is impractical due to space, thermal, and reliability constraints, and no prior art demonstrates such integration.

the testable prediction does not specify how vibration is measured, sensor location, sampling duration, or the exact definition of the 0.5 g RMS limit, leaving the hypothesis undefined and unverifiable.
